name: Embaloh
confidence_why: Irawan et al. 2024, the only dedicated prosodic study of Embaloh (twelve speakers, Praat measurements, stress unmoved by affixation), find fixed non-distinctive stress on the final syllable, but they themselves report that Adelaar 1995 and Buu 2009 placed Embaloh word stress on the penultimate syllable, and Adelaar's statement, from the leading specialist on the Tamanic languages, could not be consulted directly.

catalog_locator: pp. 28-29 (Results: Word Prosody; pp. 7-8; Fig. 2 [bukut] and ex. (1a-c) on p. 29); p. 35 (Discussion; p. 14); p. 37 (Conclusion; p. 16); second-hand report of Adelaar 1995 / Buu 2009 = penultimate on p. 24; enclitic -lah on p. 34. p.1 = journal p.22.
catalog_quote: Most of the word stress in the Embaloh language is located on the right (right edge). However, the stress is not distinctive or distinguishes the lexical meaning. The location of the lexical stress in the Embaloh language is generally in the final syllable. [...] In the Embaloh language, stress is generally consistent at the final syllable. The stress does not shift when the target word is affixed. For example, in polysyllabic (three syllables) words, the stress remains in the last syllable. Example (1a) ‒ (1c) shows that affixation does not affect the position of stress. [...] (1) a. [bu’kut] [mamu’kut] “punch” “to punch” [...] b. [ju’lu] [julu’ang] [taju’lu] “push” “to push” “pushed” [...] The location of the stress or accent of the word is not affected by the number of syllables or the affixation process. The Embaloh language is more accurately categorised as fixed-stressed because the word stress tends to be consistent in the last syllable. [...] This finding also differs from Adelaar (1995), which stated that word stress location in the Embaloh language was at the penultimate syllable. [...] At the prosodic lexical level, we conclude that the Embaloh language is fixed-stressed. It cannot be categorised as a tone language. The word stress in the Embaloh language is in the final syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (non-contrastive) falls on the final syllable of the word, including affixed/suffixed forms (stress stays word-final, i.e. moves onto a suffix); realised as an L-to-H rise of c. 3-4 semitones plus greater duration/intensity; the language is not tonal. NOTE: the older primary description (Adelaar 1995, as reported by these authors and by Buu 2009) says penultimate; the 2024 instrumental study explicitly contradicts it.
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level (stress 'generally'/'tends to be' final; number of syllables and affixation do not affect it). At phrase level: in yes/no questions with the obligatory final particle ka and in statements with the enclitic -lah, the nuclear pitch accent sits on the last syllable of the pre-final word rather than utterance-finally.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical level analysed from elicited words (Swadesh-based list, 449 items) and words in carrier/spontaneous utterances from 12 speakers of Banua Ujung (Embaloh Hulu); authors separate word stress from post-lexical pitch accent, but word-level evidence is F0/duration on words that may be utterance-final, so a boundary-tone confound is possible. Contradiction with Adelaar 1995 (penultimate) is acknowledged by the authors; Adelaar's own wording not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Irawan et al. 2024 recorded speakers in Banua Ujung village, Embaloh Hulu subdistrict, Kapuas Hulu (the Embaloh-river variety = Tamambaloh); same language as Glottolog emba1238 / ISO emb (also called Maloh). Adelaar's 1995 data are also Embaloh proper. No dialect split is coded in Glottolog.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Irawan et al. 2024, instrumental study; fixed-unreviewed) = stress on the FINAL syllable, non-distinctive, not shifted by affixation. Adelaar 1995 = PENULTIMATE syllable, non-distinctive. The two agree that stress is non-contrastive/predictable but differ in placement (penult vs final). Irawan et al. 2024 themselves report Adelaar 1995 (and Buu 2009) as penultimate on their p. 24 and state on p. 35 that their final-stress finding 'differs from Adelaar (1995)'. So this is a known source disagreement, not a transcription error; the older statement is impressionistic, the newer one acoustic.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is not contrastive (impressionistic statement in a one-paragraph phonology synopsis; no further conditions visible in the snippets).

new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar 1995 describes Embaloh proper (spoken along the Embaloh/Ambalo and Palin tributaries of the upper Kapuas, West Kalimantan), which he calls one of the three main Tamanic dialects (the others, Taman and Kalis, are named only in a footnote); Irawan et al. 2024 recorded Embaloh (Tamambaloh) speakers in Kapuas Hulu. Same language (emba1238); no dialect split explains the penult/final disagreement on the evidence available.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, secondhand: Irawan et al. 2024 (the only source actually read, already the catalog's existing statement) find fixed final-syllable, non-distinctive stress from an instrumental study, and state explicitly (p.35, p.14) that this 'differs from Adelaar (1995), which stated that word stress location in the Embaloh language was at the penultimate syllable'; on p.24 they also attribute penultimate non-distinctive stress to Buu 2009. Adelaar 1995 itself could not be opened by any open route, so the penultimate claim rests only on Irawan's paraphrase; the catalog's final-stress record stands on the one primary source that was read. Adelaar 1995 (sec. 2.1, p. 376 inferred; read only as verbatim archive.org full-text-search snippets) says 'Stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is not distinctive', whereas the catalog record for Embaloh (Irawan et al. 2024, Issues in Language Studies 13(1), acoustic study, read in full earlier) finds stress consistently on the FINAL syllable, non-distinctive and not shifted by affixation. The disagreement is on placement only (penult vs final); both call stress non-contrastive. Irawan et al. 2024 report Adelaar's penultimate claim (p. 24, with Buu 2009) and explicitly state that their result differs from it (p. 35), so the catalog's fixed: final syllable record already rests on the source that knows of and rejects the older impressionistic statement

sources.note: Instrumental (Praat, AM framework, 12 speakers, Banua Ujung / Embaloh Hulu): word stress is non-distinctive and falls on the FINAL syllable, does not shift under affixation ([bu'kut] ~ [mamu'kut], [ju'lu] ~ [julu'ang] ~ [taju'lu]); language classed as fixed-stress, right-edge, not tonal (pp. 29-30, 35, 37). Also reports (p. 25) that Adelaar 1995 and Buu 2009 give penultimate non-distinctive stress, and explicitly says its finding differs from Adelaar 1995 (p. 35).
